content.content:
1	# Specification page: design review, reconciliation and requirements
2	
3	Status: ANALYSIS ONLY. No page was changed while writing this. Source: every statement the owner made about the
4	specification pages in the 2026-10-29 session (quoted in section 1), plus the reference sites and articles named.
5	Purpose: settle what the owner actually requires, resolve the places where the feedback pulls in opposite
6	directions, and state tenets and acceptance tests, so the next redesign starts from a fixed baseline instead of
7	another round of restyling.
8	
9	## 1. The record (grouped, in the owner's words)
10	
11	**Content and meaning of values**
12	- "I need exhaustive jurisdiction comparisons ... accordion drop-downs ... top line is the jurisdiction and the salient standard/clause/value/note, and then an expansion upon everything below."
13	- "A-01 ... far too vague with value of 800-1300mm. who on earth is that 800-1300mm for?" / "'ALL' is fine, but we need to have specific populations too" / "ALL is basically the same as saying it is universal" / "then we have population/code/need specific and then person specific."
14	- "'Mode P' is jargon for users." / "'WHY IT MATTERS' needs to have line breaks, and it should be using bullet points."
15	- "we do not need to have rows for people where the value is just 'Not set.' that just means that it shouldn't be showing on the page."
16	- "how on earth do we have evidence outside the library? we either have evidence or we do not have evidence."
17	- "You do not need to find evidence for why 1:12 was the code floor--just accept the 1:12 as a baseline." / "if you can't find evidence for why a T4-T6 is why it is, that is fine."
18	- "We are interested in what are best practices NOW ... we do not need to interrogate the history."
19	- "do not include countries outside of the major identified countries for now." Buckets 1 and 2: "canada usa australia japan norway etc then like italy china whatever" (the repo's P1+P2+P3 was adopted).
20	
21	**Tools and interaction**
22	- "you should be able to select units for each page, ie metric vs imperial, % slope vs ratio slope vs degrees."
23	- "we also need to be able to sort page by population/ICF code/access need" (restated: filter).
24	- Filter by one of three lenses; "when you select which lens do you see the pills pop up with the more specific case"; "we don't want to show ALL the pills at once"; "the filters shouldn't start out expanded ... the three lens filters ... are their own row, and when you click one, there is a new row beneath that has the different pills."
25	- "think about how ... shopping websites make judicious uses of filters where you can filter for colours, prices, sizes ... and then the subsequent more granular items if desired."
26	- "for ramp gradient, i want there to also be an easy comparison master table where you just see what each jurisdiction has for the value"; "you can click on value for a popup or an anchor location or as its own subpage."
27	- "you don't need to show the full jurisdiction standard's name in a column ... on its own full span row below ... smaller italicized text."
28	
29	**Evidence and citation**
30	- "all of these references 'In the library' to be in APA format with author/body and year ... clickable and pop-up the bibliographic citation and then list all pages where it has been cited under the entry."
31	- "evidence in the library needs to be sorted alphabetically by last name" and "ideally it is subcategorized by population group/access need/icf code (depends upon filter chosen up top)."
32	
33	**Research method (shapes the page's content, not its look)**
34	- "our goal is to be looking at all the bucket 1+2 jurisdictions for what they do with ramps, and then ... what academic studies and professional bodies and advocacy groups recommend."
35	- "the critical methodology comes from synthesis/adjudication/specifications, not from evidence collection."
36	- "ensure that we are correctly scraping all information ... from the most recent codes and standards ... and then we move on to higher tier evidence ... across any language in any jurisdiction ... to see if there are even better approaches that go beyond those codes."
37	
38	**Visual design and hierarchy**
39	- "I do not like how VALUES is set up ... we don't need to have so many headings and fonts and pills and stuff. this needs to be radically simplified, and we need to make a lot more use of accordions and pop-up pills."
40	- "think about how dimensions.com presents information ... make the actually salient information/values highly visible and easy to read without needing to spend time reading large lengths of texts."
41	- "too much page space" (filters/controls); "uses up too much page space."
42	- "sections do not cleanly separate or have breaks, section headers lack weight or real dynamic identification, too much disparity and breaking logic for font sizes and weights for hierarchy of information."
43	- "that needs to be way less yellow, and i really dislike the typefaces used and the size hierarchy sucks. the book-era is better for how info is organized not necessarily for style."
44	- "too many AI design tropes" ... "wikipedia is very good and simple, dimensions.com is very good and simple, substack is very good and simple. the idea is to make this as clearly presented and formatted as possible with information as primary." References given: UX Collective, Medium/PicsRush (not readable: HTTP 403), Bright Avenue, JSTOR (bot challenge; the saved copy is script-rendered), Wiley (403).
45	- On the Wikipedia-style version: "oh no that is not good at all"; "i don't want it to look like wikipedia"; "the point of wikipedia is that it is very clearly organized"; "the previous design iteration was a lot lot better but the organization of information in this one is much improved ... so far worse aesthetics, better data flow."
46	- "refer to swiss graphic design." "look at this example [dimensions.com single-hung windows] ... very simple, very clear."
47	- Review "across different formats and sizes and ratios from landscape to portrait."
48	
49	## 2. What the references actually say (so the analysis rests on evidence)
50	
51	- **UX Collective (read):** minimalism is a choice about priorities, not a shortage of design; keep only what helps the visitor reach the goal; one or two typefaces; a clear size difference between headings and body; neutral tones plus a single accent; generous space around key content and tighter space to group; do not use light grey on white for body text; test on phones; keep primary navigation visible.
52	- **Bright Avenue (read):** every element needs a reason to be there; two or three core colours plus one accent; one consistent link colour; visitors skim, so use headings, short sections, bullets, and bold or italics for key facts; keep menus short and labels specific; **do not go too minimal or clinical and do not remove content**; keep a sticky header if people need to move around.
53	- **Medium/PicsRush, JSTOR, Wiley:** could not be read (403 or bot challenge). The saved JSTOR file is script-rendered; its CSS names a design system and a single sans-serif, white ground, grey rules and one blue accent (#3860be). Nothing else can be claimed about these three.
54	- **Wikipedia, Substack (from general knowledge, not fetched here):** Wikipedia: content visible by default, a lead then an infobox of key facts, plain hairline tables, numbered references, single-pixel heading rules. Substack: one narrow reading column, large calm type, nothing at the sides.
55	- **dimensions.com (page seen):** a large illustration first, then plainly labelled sections ("Description", "History"), short paragraphs, one hue, one typeface. The collection page I could see is prose-led and has no value table, so what the owner values there is its **calm and clarity**, not a particular table layout. I have not seen an individual dimension page; if that is what the owner means, I need that link.
56	- **Swiss graphic design (principles):** modular grid, asymmetric layout, flush-left ragged-right text, one neo-grotesque sans (Helvetica or Akzidenz), hierarchy from size and weight alone, thin rules, generous space, objective content, restrained colour (often black, white and one red).
57	
58	## 3. Themes
59	
60	1. **Information is primary.** The reader should see the answer without reading prose or operating controls.
61	2. **Organisation is the thing to get right first.** The owner separates "how info is organized" (valued, book-era and the article iteration) from "style" (to be neutral and subordinate).
62	3. **Depth on demand.** Complete, exhaustive information must exist but sit behind accordions and popups; the top line carries only the salient figure.
63	4. **Meaning of every value is explicit.** Who it is for, in which tier, with which source; no jargon; no empty rows; no pseudo-evidence.
64	5. **Traceability and scholarship.** APA citations, popups, cited-on lists, alphabetical and lens-grouped evidence.
65	6. **Compact, on-demand controls.** Units and filters are essential but must not consume page space; pills appear only after a lens is chosen.
66	7. **One disciplined visual system.** Few sizes and weights, one typeface, near-neutral colour, strong section separation, no decoration.
67	8. **Fit for any screen.** Portrait to landscape, phone to wide desktop, no horizontal scroll, readable tables.
68	9. **Scope discipline.** Major countries only, current editions only, code values accepted as baselines.
69	
70	## 4. Conflicts and how each is resolved
71	
72	| # | Apparent conflict | Resolution |
73	|---|---|---|
74	| C1 | "Radically simplify ... fewer pills" vs "a lot more use of accordions and pop-up pills" | Different jobs. Primary answers are never collapsed. Accordions and popups hold depth (jurisdiction detail, basis, citation). Pills exist only as filter options, shown on demand, never as status or decoration. |
75	| C2 | "I don't want it to look like Wikipedia" vs "wikipedia is very good ... the point is that it is very clearly organized" | Take Wikipedia's organisation (lead, key facts, plain tables, content visible, numbered references), not its skin (blue links, grey panels, contents box, framed tables). |
76	| C3 | "Previous iteration ... a lot lot better" aesthetics vs "this one ... better data flow" | Combine: previous iteration's look (white, one sans, numbered sections with a heavy rule, sticky section nav, hero value) on the article iteration's information order. |
77	| C4 | Minimal ("too many AI tropes", "radically simplified") vs "section headers lack weight or real dynamic identification" | Minimal is not flat. Strong, consistent hierarchy is required; identification comes from position, number, rule and weight, not colour tints. Bright Avenue's warning against over-minimalism supports this. |
78	| C5 | Book era for organisation, Swiss/dimensions/Substack for style | Two layers: information architecture (book-era table-first, value-first) fixed first; visual skin (Swiss grid, one sans, neutral) applied second and held neutral. |
79	| C6 | Exhaustive comparisons vs "too much page space" and "major countries only" | Exhaustive within scope: one row per major jurisdiction (24), everything else behind the row. Countries outside scope are not shown. |
80	| C7 | "Far more information" vs "without needing to spend time reading large lengths of texts" | Structured fields (value, unit, when, source) over prose; first sentence only on the surface; full text one click away. |
81	| C8 | Shopping-style filters vs "too much page space" and "don't show all pills" | Filter facets collapsed behind three lens buttons; applied filters shown as a short removable line; counts shown; results regroup by lens. |
82	| C9 | Units selector required vs compact controls | Two compact controls (length, slope) plus one filter row; everything else hidden until used. |
83	| C10 | "Dimensions.com is very simple" vs the page seen being prose-heavy with section pill labels | The shared quality is calm clarity and a visual first. Do not copy its decoration; do copy a clear lead visual and consistent plain section labels. Open question Q3. |
84	
85	## 5. Tenets (in order of precedence)
86	
87	1. **Information first.** If an element does not help the reader find or trust a value, remove it.
88	2. **Answer within the first screen.** The Guidebook value, the common legal range and the start of the comparison are visible with no interaction, on desktop and on a phone.
89	3. **Organise, then style.** The information order is fixed before any visual choice, and the skin never changes the order.
90	4. **Salient values large, labels small, prose short.** One idea per line; first sentence on the surface.
91	5. **One visual system.** One sans-serif family, at most four type sizes, each role using the same size in every section, two weights, black and white plus greys, at most one accent used only for state (active, focus, hit). No decoration: no tiles, status pills, shadows, rounded boxes, gradients, tinted sections, uppercase tracked labels, icons or emoji.
92	6. **Structure is visible.** Sections separate with space and a rule; each heading is numbered and heavy; a nav shows where you are.
93	7. **Evidence is binary and traceable.** Recorded or absent. Every figure leads to a citation; every citation lists where it is used.
94	8. **Scope is explicit.** Major jurisdictions, current editions, T4-T6 values accepted as baselines.
95	9. **Responsive by structure.** Tables re-flow rather than scroll; touch targets at least 44 px.
96	10. **Accessible, always.** (Owner, mid-session: "all work must comply with website accessibility standards and best practices.") WCAG 2.2 level AA is the floor, with the cognitive (COGA) guidance the project already adopted in `governance/armature_v3_review.md` §6. Accessibility is a precondition for every other tenet, not a trade-off against them; where a design choice and an accessibility rule conflict, the rule wins.
97	
98	## 6. Requirements with acceptance tests
99	
100	**Information architecture (fixed order)**
101	- R1. Order: title and one-line question; hero of three figures (Guidebook value, most common legal maximum, gentlest); compact units and filter row; 1 Specification (who / value / short basis); 2 Requirements by jurisdiction (master table, then details); 3 Why it matters (bullets); 4 Evidence (APA list); 5 Gaps; 6 About this page. Test: a reader finds the Guidebook value and the 1:12 range with no scrolling at 1280x800 and 375x812.
102	- R2. Master table: one row per major jurisdiction; columns Preferred, Maximum (and when), Between landings; standard name, edition and verification on a small italic full-width line beneath each row; click a value for the detail popup; sortable by maximum. Test: 24 jurisdictions in scope; none outside scope appear.
103	- R3. Value tiers: everyone, specific group / ICF / access need, one person; each row says who it is for; rows with no value are not rendered. Test: no row contains "Not set".
104	- R4. No jargon and no "outside the library" language. Test: text search finds neither.
105	
106	**Tools**
107	- R5. Two unit controls (length; slope) apply to every figure, including drawings and popups.
108	- R6. Filter: three lens buttons in one row; pills only after a lens is chosen and only for that lens; counts on options; applied filters as a removable line; evidence regroups by the chosen lens (population group, ICF chapter, or need).
109	- R7. Controls block no taller than about 100 px on desktop and landscape phone, and about 190 px on a phone, when collapsed.
110	
111	**Evidence**
112	- R8. Evidence is an APA reference list, alphabetical by first author's last name (organisation name for corporate authors); each entry opens a popup with the full citation and the list of pages that cite it, and shows "Cited on" under the entry.
113	- R9. Why it matters is bullets, one or two short sentences each.
114	
115	**Visual**
116	- R10. Type: one sans-serif family (Helvetica/Arial class; no web fonts, no monospace), four sizes with one job each in every section: 56 (36 on phones) page title; 24 section headings, headline figures, the question and dialog titles; 16 all body text, table cells, list items and controls; 13 all secondary text (qualifiers, standard names, captions, labels, table column heads). Weights 400 and 700 only. In tables the value is 16 bold, the row label 16 regular, everything secondary 13 regular. Test: computed styles show one family, at most five sizes and two weights.
117	- R11. Colour: white ground, black text, two greys, hairline grey rules; no yellow or cream tint anywhere; one accent for state only. Test: at most four text colours; no background tints except a light grey for hit rows.
118	- R12. Structure: numbered section headings with a heavy top rule and consistent spacing; a sticky nav that marks the current section; consistent hover and focus states.
119	- R13. Grid: a 12-column grid, flush-left text, asymmetric layout (section titles in a left rail, content in the right nine columns), collapsing to one column below about 760 px.
120	
121	**Responsive and quality**
122	- R14. No horizontal page scroll at 375, 768, 812x375, 1024, 1280 and 1920 wide; tables restructure on narrow screens; page length budget about 6,000 px at desktop with details collapsed.
123	- R15. Accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA minimum; project standard per `governance/armature_v3_review.md`; prior site audit `audits/accessibility-audit-2026-05-10.md`). Itemised in section 6a. Each item is a pass/fail test and must pass before a page is shown to the owner.
124	
125	### 6a. Accessibility requirements (testable)
126	
127	**Perceivable**
128	- A1. Text contrast at least 4.5:1 (large text 3:1); non-text UI (control borders, focus ring, chart lines) at least 3:1 (1.4.3, 1.4.11). Check light and dark schemes separately.
129	- A2. No information by colour alone (1.4.1): a pressed filter, active section or highlighted row also changes weight, underline or a marker; any status uses words, not only a symbol.
130	- A3. Reflow (1.4.10): usable at 320 CSS px with no horizontal scroll of the page; 200% and 400% zoom without loss of content (1.4.4); user text-spacing overrides do not clip (1.4.12).
131	- A4. Semantics (1.3.1, 1.3.2): one `h1`; headings never skip a level; data in real `<table>` with `<caption>` or an accessible name, `<th scope>`; lists are lists; reading order equals visual order. When a table is restyled for narrow screens, header association must survive (do not hide `thead` with `display:none` without supplying equivalent names).
132	- A5. Figures and drawings: every SVG has an accessible name and a text equivalent (a short description plus the data as a table or list); drawing text uses real text so the unit selector and zoom work.
133	- A6. Language (3.1.1, 3.1.2): `lang` on the page and on foreign-language strings (for example the Japanese standard title).
134	- A7. Honour `prefers-color-scheme`, `prefers-reduced-motion` and forced-colors (no motion is required by the design; transitions off when reduced).
135	
136	**Operable**
137	- A8. Everything works by keyboard alone (2.1.1), no trap (2.1.2), logical focus order (2.4.3), visible focus on every control at 3:1 or better (2.4.7, 2.4.13 where applicable).
138	- A9. Focus not obscured (2.4.11): a sticky nav must not cover a focused element (use `scroll-padding-top` or avoid sticky).
139	- A10. Skip link to the main content is the first focusable element (2.4.1); descriptive page title and link text (2.4.2, 2.4.4); section nav marks the current section with `aria-current`.
140	- A11. Target size at least 24x24 CSS px (2.5.8); the design aims for 44 px on touch. No drag-only interaction (2.5.7).
141	- A12. Dialogs: native `<dialog>` with `showModal`, a visible and labelled close control, Escape closes, focus moves in on open and returns to the invoking control on close; background inert. Content that appears on hover or focus is dismissible, hoverable and persistent (1.4.13); the design uses click, not hover.
142	- A13. No time limits and no auto-updating content; filter changes announce the result count through a polite live region (4.1.3).
143	
144	**Understandable**
145	- A14. Every control has a visible label and a programmatic name; unit selectors are labelled `select` elements; toggle buttons use `aria-pressed`; accordions are native `details/summary`.
146	- A15. Consistent navigation and consistent identification of repeated components (3.2.3, 3.2.4); no change of context on input.
147	- A16. Plain language (COGA): short sentences, no unexplained jargon or codes (ICF and need codes are always shown with their names), the same term for the same thing throughout; abbreviations expanded on first use; values always carry their unit and who they apply to.
148	
149	**Robust**
150	- A17. Valid HTML; name, role and state exposed for every custom control (4.1.2); no `title`-only information; no ARIA where a native element does the job.
151	
152	**Verification before sign-off**
153	- V1. Automated scan (axe-core and Lighthouse accessibility) with zero violations at the sizes in R14.
154	- V2. Keyboard-only walkthrough of every task: change units, apply and clear a filter, open and close a value popup and a citation popup, expand a jurisdiction.
155	- V3. Screen-reader spot check (NVDA with Firefox or Chrome; VoiceOver where available) of the master table, a popup and a filtered view.
156	- V4. 320 px and 400% zoom pass; forced-colors and dark-scheme pass; printed output readable.
157	- V5. Record results in an accessibility audit file next to this one. Findings are never self-certified as compliant; a "pass" means the specific tests above passed on the date and build recorded.
158	
159	### 6b. Known accessibility defects in earlier iterations (do not repeat)
160	- Narrow-screen CSS hid table headers with `display:none`, breaking column-header association for screen readers (A4).
161	- A sticky section nav with no `scroll-padding` could obscure focused elements (A9).
162	- Verification was shown with filled and open circles and a tooltip (`title`) only (A2, A17).
163	- The Japanese standard title had no `lang` attribute (A6).
164	- The gradient drawing had only an `aria-label`, no text equivalent (A5).
165	- Dotted-underline button text for values and citations gave a weak, non-standard link affordance and relied on hover (A1, A8).
166	- None of the iterations has been run through an automated or screen-reader test (V1-V3).
167	
168	## 7. Where each iteration stands against this
169	
170	| Iteration | Strengths | Fails |
171	|---|---|---|
172	| 1. Original v2 page (own CSS, three typefaces, tiles, pills, 26 type combinations) | Content depth; units; filters; citations | R10, R11, R12; far too long; horizontal scroll at 768 |
173	| 2. v3 on the site stylesheet (cream, slab and mono) | Section identity; consistent with the site | Owner dislikes the typefaces and the yellow; sizes poor (R10, R11) |
174	| 3. Neutral version (white, one sans, numbered heavy-rule sections, sticky nav, hero) | Aesthetics the owner preferred; R10-R12 mostly met | Information order and tables less clear than iteration 4 |
175	| 4. Article version (Wikipedia-like organisation) | Information order, plain tables, content visible: "better data flow" | Skin: blue links, grey panels and boxes, contents box; owner rejected the look |
176	| 5. Swiss-grid version (built, not yet reviewed with the owner) | Fits R13 | Untested against R1-R15; not yet judged by the owner |
177	
178	## 8. Decisions needed from the owner before redesign
179	
180	- Q1. Typeface: is one neo-grotesque (Helvetica/Arial) the intended Swiss reference, or do you prefer another single sans (for example a system UI sans)? A serif body is off the table unless you say otherwise.
181	- Q2. Accent: Swiss red for state only, a dark blue, or none (black and grey only)?
182	- Q3. Dimensions.com: the page I saw is a prose-led collection page. Is there a specific dimension page whose value display you want to match?
183	- Q4. Lead graphic: do you want a drawing under the hero on every spec page (the draft drew the run needed for the same rise at each gradient from the page's own data)? It carries the data visually but needs a data-driven drawing per item.
184	- Q5. Sticky section nav: keep it (it gives "dynamic identification") or drop it on short pages?
185	- Q6. Default state of jurisdiction details and evidence notes: collapsed (shortest page) or expanded?
186	- Q7. Dark mode: required, or ignore for now?
187	
188	## 9. Process notes (what I got wrong)
189	
190	- I restyled five times without a fixed requirements baseline, so each pass answered the last remark and undid an earlier one.
191	- I applied the site stylesheet before checking whether the owner liked it, and treated "Wikipedia is good" as a skin rather than an organisation.
192	- I gave weight to references I could not read (Medium, JSTOR, Wiley) as if I had; nothing here relies on them except the saved JSTOR file's design-system facts.
193	
194	## 10. Doctrine alignment (added after reading the mission and project doctrines)
195	
196	Documents read: `governance/mission-and-epistemics.md` (CANONICAL), `governance/audience-priority.md` (CANONICAL),
197	`references/project-standards.md` Core Doctrine, `governance/tier-system.md`.
198	
199	**Owner definition of best practice (stated in session, matches the Core Doctrine rule):** the Guidebook takes no
200	positions. Best practice is the best way to do something according to how it benefits the intended group, determined by
201	the evidence hierarchy, not by code consensus and not by what is most common. For a given item and group the page shows
202	the most accommodating value found (here the gentlest slope, 1:20, which is gentler than Germany's 1:16.7 maximum) and
203	whether any study or professional body improves on it. Codes are shown as the regulatory minimum for comparison.
204	
205	Changes made in the page to match:
206	- Removed "Guidebook position", "working position", "most common legal maximum" and the steepest-slope figure (owner: do not highlight it). The hero shows the best practice found and the gentlest legal maximum.
207	- Evidence markers are shown on every value row (project rule: unmarked is an error): the symbol plus the words "evidence-based" or "inferred", with a legend; symbol alone is never relied on (accessibility A2).
208	- Wording follows the specification-language rule (the project is an advocacy project, not a standard-setting body): no "shall be" or "must"; the person tier reads "An occupational therapist's assessment determines the position within the range"; basis lines say what the standards and studies state.
209	- Values are marked provisional: the best-practice value rests on standards alone (tier 4 to 6), and no higher-tier study sets a value.
210	- Populations with no evidence stay off the table (owner instruction) but are named in the Gaps section, so the page is not silent about them.
211	- The page states that no lived-experience (Co-1) evidence on this item is recorded in the library (checked in the database: 0 Co-1 sources linked to the item's evidence base; the library holds 29 Co-1 sources overall, none on ramps or slopes).
212	- The controls (lens, filters, units) sit above all information, as the owner required. The question line under the title was removed at the owner's direction ("irrelevant"), so this page no longer carries a question at all.
213	
214	**Tensions between the owner's instructions and the written doctrine (need an owner decision, not silently resolved):**
215	1. Evidence-state rule says a cell with sparse evidence displays `[BEST-PRACTICE-PENDING]` with a gap link. The owner said rows that are "Not set" should not show. Current handling: no table row, a plain statement in Gaps. Confirm.
216	2. Doctrine says tier 4 to 6 are a regulatory baseline "walled off from best-practice anchoring" and that a best-practice claim from standards alone is "in error" when it comes from convergence. The owner's rule (best practice is the most accommodating value stated by a current standard unless evidence improves on it) is implemented as a single-source gentlest value, marked evidence-based but provisional, with the basis stated. Confirm this is the intended reading and whether the marker should be inferred instead.
217	3. The questions-led commitment ("questions are first-class data") is not met on this page: the owner removed the question line under the title as irrelevant, and there is no "questions to ask" content for E-03 in the data (none invented). Confirm how the questions-led doctrine should appear on specification pages.
218	4. Audience-priority doctrine names four audiences and use-patterns; the site's exemplar `specs/e-08.html` has a "Reading as" lens that changes which sections open by default. It has not been built into this page. The three owner lenses (population, ICF code, access need) are all present. Confirm whether the audience lens is wanted here.
219	5. Doctrine requires within-population variability as a first-class dimension; the page shows it only through the person tier and group rows. More is possible once data exists.
220	
221	
222	Control order (owner, 2026-10-29): the Lens row comes first, then its pills when a lens is chosen, then the Units row; all controls sit above all information.
223	
224	## 11. Addendum: navigation legibility (owner, 2026-10-30)
225	Owner: "ensure that minimalism does not come at the expense of readability/legibility especially as it pertains to accessibility practices for website navigation."
226	- R16. Navigation (breadcrumb, section nav, skip links, disclosure and sort controls) is at least as large and as dark as body text (16 px or larger, near-black on white, or the dark-scheme equivalent); the current location is marked at page load; control state (open, closed, sorted, pressed) is visible without relying on small grey glyphs; targets are at least 44 px high on touch screens. Tenet: minimalism removes decoration, never legibility or state cues.
227	- Pills are allowed if used judiciously (filter options, applied filters); decorative or status pills remain the trope to avoid.
228	- Defects against these rules are listed in `audits/spec-page-design-defects-2026-10-30.md` section E.
229	
230	
231	## 12. Owner answers to the open doctrine questions (2026-10-30)
232	- Pending cells: unchanged (no "Not set" rows; gaps listed under Gaps).
233	- Standards as best practice: the owner decided that the gentlest value found in practice is best practice and that no academic study is required; the mission document's tier 4 to 6 wall is therefore superseded in practice and needs a decision record (D-DOCT).
234	- Provisional means the source reading needs a second review; page wording corrected accordingly.
235	- "Covered" means read, extracted and verified; the page now says "read, none yet verified" and lists uncovered jurisdictions as "not yet read".
236	- Two lenses exist: audience and disability. The audience lens is not yet built on the v3 page.
237	- All spec pages now live in `site/specs/` (the root `specs/` folder was removed; `index.html` links and the e-08 exemplar's relative paths were updated).

# Specification page: design review, reconciliation and requirements

Status: ANALYSIS ONLY. No page was changed while writing this. Source: every statement the owner made about the
specification pages in the 2026-10-29 session (quoted in section 1), plus the reference sites and articles named.
Purpose: settle what the owner actually requires, resolve the places where the feedback pulls in opposite
directions, and state tenets and acceptance tests, so the next redesign starts from a fixed baseline instead of
another round of restyling.

## 1. The record (grouped, in the owner's words)

**Content and meaning of values**
- "I need exhaustive jurisdiction comparisons ... accordion drop-downs ... top line is the jurisdiction and the salient standard/clause/value/note, and then an expansion upon everything below."
- "A-01 ... far too vague with value of 800-1300mm. who on earth is that 800-1300mm for?" / "'ALL' is fine, but we need to have specific populations too" / "ALL is basically the same as saying it is universal" / "then we have population/code/need specific and then person specific."
- "'Mode P' is jargon for users." / "'WHY IT MATTERS' needs to have line breaks, and it should be using bullet points."
- "we do not need to have rows for people where the value is just 'Not set.' that just means that it shouldn't be showing on the page."
- "how on earth do we have evidence outside the library? we either have evidence or we do not have evidence."
- "You do not need to find evidence for why 1:12 was the code floor--just accept the 1:12 as a baseline." / "if you can't find evidence for why a T4-T6 is why it is, that is fine."
- "We are interested in what are best practices NOW ... we do not need to interrogate the history."
- "do not include countries outside of the major identified countries for now." Buckets 1 and 2: "canada usa australia japan norway etc then like italy china whatever" (the repo's P1+P2+P3 was adopted).

**Tools and interaction**
- "you should be able to select units for each page, ie metric vs imperial, % slope vs ratio slope vs degrees."
- "we also need to be able to sort page by population/ICF code/access need" (restated: filter).
- Filter by one of three lenses; "when you select which lens do you see the pills pop up with the more specific case"; "we don't want to show ALL the pills at once"; "the filters shouldn't start out expanded ... the three lens filters ... are their own row, and when you click one, there is a new row beneath that has the different pills."
- "think about how ... shopping websites make judicious uses of filters where you can filter for colours, prices, sizes ... and then the subsequent more granular items if desired."
- "for ramp gradient, i want there to also be an easy comparison master table where you just see what each jurisdiction has for the value"; "you can click on value for a popup or an anchor location or as its own subpage."
- "you don't need to show the full jurisdiction standard's name in a column ... on its own full span row below ... smaller italicized text."

**Evidence and citation**
- "all of these references 'In the library' to be in APA format with author/body and year ... clickable and pop-up the bibliographic citation and then list all pages where it has been cited under the entry."
- "evidence in the library needs to be sorted alphabetically by last name" and "ideally it is subcategorized by population group/access need/icf code (depends upon filter chosen up top)."

**Research method (shapes the page's content, not its look)**
- "our goal is to be looking at all the bucket 1+2 jurisdictions for what they do with ramps, and then ... what academic studies and professional bodies and advocacy groups recommend."
- "the critical methodology comes from synthesis/adjudication/specifications, not from evidence collection."
- "ensure that we are correctly scraping all information ... from the most recent codes and standards ... and then we move on to higher tier evidence ... across any language in any jurisdiction ... to see if there are even better approaches that go beyond those codes."

**Visual design and hierarchy**
- "I do not like how VALUES is set up ... we don't need to have so many headings and fonts and pills and stuff. this needs to be radically simplified, and we need to make a lot more use of accordions and pop-up pills."
- "think about how dimensions.com presents information ... make the actually salient information/values highly visible and easy to read without needing to spend time reading large lengths of texts."
- "too much page space" (filters/controls); "uses up too much page space."
- "sections do not cleanly separate or have breaks, section headers lack weight or real dynamic identification, too much disparity and breaking logic for font sizes and weights for hierarchy of information."
- "that needs to be way less yellow, and i really dislike the typefaces used and the size hierarchy sucks. the book-era is better for how info is organized not necessarily for style."
- "too many AI design tropes" ... "wikipedia is very good and simple, dimensions.com is very good and simple, substack is very good and simple. the idea is to make this as clearly presented and formatted as possible with information as primary." References given: UX Collective, Medium/PicsRush (not readable: HTTP 403), Bright Avenue, JSTOR (bot challenge; the saved copy is script-rendered), Wiley (403).
- On the Wikipedia-style version: "oh no that is not good at all"; "i don't want it to look like wikipedia"; "the point of wikipedia is that it is very clearly organized"; "the previous design iteration was a lot lot better but the organization of information in this one is much improved ... so far worse aesthetics, better data flow."
- "refer to swiss graphic design." "look at this example [dimensions.com single-hung windows] ... very simple, very clear."
- Review "across different formats and sizes and ratios from landscape to portrait."

## 2. What the references actually say (so the analysis rests on evidence)

- **UX Collective (read):** minimalism is a choice about priorities, not a shortage of design; keep only what helps the visitor reach the goal; one or two typefaces; a clear size difference between headings and body; neutral tones plus a single accent; generous space around key content and tighter space to group; do not use light grey on white for body text; test on phones; keep primary navigation visible.
- **Bright Avenue (read):** every element needs a reason to be there; two or three core colours plus one accent; one consistent link colour; visitors skim, so use headings, short sections, bullets, and bold or italics for key facts; keep menus short and labels specific; **do not go too minimal or clinical and do not remove content**; keep a sticky header if people need to move around.
- **Medium/PicsRush, JSTOR, Wiley:** could not be read (403 or bot challenge). The saved JSTOR file is script-rendered; its CSS names a design system and a single sans-serif, white ground, grey rules and one blue accent (#3860be). Nothing else can be claimed about these three.
- **Wikipedia, Substack (from general knowledge, not fetched here):** Wikipedia: content visible by default, a lead then an infobox of key facts, plain hairline tables, numbered references, single-pixel heading rules. Substack: one narrow reading column, large calm type, nothing at the sides.
- **dimensions.com (page seen):** a large illustration first, then plainly labelled sections ("Description", "History"), short paragraphs, one hue, one typeface. The collection page I could see is prose-led and has no value table, so what the owner values there is its **calm and clarity**, not a particular table layout. I have not seen an individual dimension page; if that is what the owner means, I need that link.
- **Swiss graphic design (principles):** modular grid, asymmetric layout, flush-left ragged-right text, one neo-grotesque sans (Helvetica or Akzidenz), hierarchy from size and weight alone, thin rules, generous space, objective content, restrained colour (often black, white and one red).

## 3. Themes

1. **Information is primary.** The reader should see the answer without reading prose or operating controls.
2. **Organisation is the thing to get right first.** The owner separates "how info is organized" (valued, book-era and the article iteration) from "style" (to be neutral and subordinate).
3. **Depth on demand.** Complete, exhaustive information must exist but sit behind accordions and popups; the top line carries only the salient figure.
4. **Meaning of every value is explicit.** Who it is for, in which tier, with which source; no jargon; no empty rows; no pseudo-evidence.
5. **Traceability and scholarship.** APA citations, popups, cited-on lists, alphabetical and lens-grouped evidence.
6. **Compact, on-demand controls.** Units and filters are essential but must not consume page space; pills appear only after a lens is chosen.
7. **One disciplined visual system.** Few sizes and weights, one typeface, near-neutral colour, strong section separation, no decoration.
8. **Fit for any screen.** Portrait to landscape, phone to wide desktop, no horizontal scroll, readable tables.
9. **Scope discipline.** Major countries only, current editions only, code values accepted as baselines.

## 4. Conflicts and how each is resolved

| # | Apparent conflict | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| C1 | "Radically simplify ... fewer pills" vs "a lot more use of accordions and pop-up pills" | Different jobs. Primary answers are never collapsed. Accordions and popups hold depth (jurisdiction detail, basis, citation). Pills exist only as filter options, shown on demand, never as status or decoration. |
| C2 | "I don't want it to look like Wikipedia" vs "wikipedia is very good ... the point is that it is very clearly organized" | Take Wikipedia's organisation (lead, key facts, plain tables, content visible, numbered references), not its skin (blue links, grey panels, contents box, framed tables). |
| C3 | "Previous iteration ... a lot lot better" aesthetics vs "this one ... better data flow" | Combine: previous iteration's look (white, one sans, numbered sections with a heavy rule, sticky section nav, hero value) on the article iteration's information order. |
| C4 | Minimal ("too many AI tropes", "radically simplified") vs "section headers lack weight or real dynamic identification" | Minimal is not flat. Strong, consistent hierarchy is required; identification comes from position, number, rule and weight, not colour tints. Bright Avenue's warning against over-minimalism supports this. |
| C5 | Book era for organisation, Swiss/dimensions/Substack for style | Two layers: information architecture (book-era table-first, value-first) fixed first; visual skin (Swiss grid, one sans, neutral) applied second and held neutral. |
| C6 | Exhaustive comparisons vs "too much page space" and "major countries only" | Exhaustive within scope: one row per major jurisdiction (24), everything else behind the row. Countries outside scope are not shown. |
| C7 | "Far more information" vs "without needing to spend time reading large lengths of texts" | Structured fields (value, unit, when, source) over prose; first sentence only on the surface; full text one click away. |
| C8 | Shopping-style filters vs "too much page space" and "don't show all pills" | Filter facets collapsed behind three lens buttons; applied filters shown as a short removable line; counts shown; results regroup by lens. |
| C9 | Units selector required vs compact controls | Two compact controls (length, slope) plus one filter row; everything else hidden until used. |
| C10 | "Dimensions.com is very simple" vs the page seen being prose-heavy with section pill labels | The shared quality is calm clarity and a visual first. Do not copy its decoration; do copy a clear lead visual and consistent plain section labels. Open question Q3. |

## 5. Tenets (in order of precedence)

1. **Information first.** If an element does not help the reader find or trust a value, remove it.
2. **Answer within the first screen.** The Guidebook value, the common legal range and the start of the comparison are visible with no interaction, on desktop and on a phone.
3. **Organise, then style.** The information order is fixed before any visual choice, and the skin never changes the order.
4. **Salient values large, labels small, prose short.** One idea per line; first sentence on the surface.
5. **One visual system.** One sans-serif family, at most four type sizes, each role using the same size in every section, two weights, black and white plus greys, at most one accent used only for state (active, focus, hit). No decoration: no tiles, status pills, shadows, rounded boxes, gradients, tinted sections, uppercase tracked labels, icons or emoji.
6. **Structure is visible.** Sections separate with space and a rule; each heading is numbered and heavy; a nav shows where you are.
7. **Evidence is binary and traceable.** Recorded or absent. Every figure leads to a citation; every citation lists where it is used.
8. **Scope is explicit.** Major jurisdictions, current editions, T4-T6 values accepted as baselines.
9. **Responsive by structure.** Tables re-flow rather than scroll; touch targets at least 44 px.
10. **Accessible, always.** (Owner, mid-session: "all work must comply with website accessibility standards and best practices.") WCAG 2.2 level AA is the floor, with the cognitive (COGA) guidance the project already adopted in `governance/armature_v3_review.md` §6. Accessibility is a precondition for every other tenet, not a trade-off against them; where a design choice and an accessibility rule conflict, the rule wins.

## 6. Requirements with acceptance tests

**Information architecture (fixed order)**
- R1. Order: title and one-line question; hero of three figures (Guidebook value, most common legal maximum, gentlest); compact units and filter row; 1 Specification (who / value / short basis); 2 Requirements by jurisdiction (master table, then details); 3 Why it matters (bullets); 4 Evidence (APA list); 5 Gaps; 6 About this page. Test: a reader finds the Guidebook value and the 1:12 range with no scrolling at 1280x800 and 375x812.
- R2. Master table: one row per major jurisdiction; columns Preferred, Maximum (and when), Between landings; standard name, edition and verification on a small italic full-width line beneath each row; click a value for the detail popup; sortable by maximum. Test: 24 jurisdictions in scope; none outside scope appear.
- R3. Value tiers: everyone, specific group / ICF / access need, one person; each row says who it is for; rows with no value are not rendered. Test: no row contains "Not set".
- R4. No jargon and no "outside the library" language. Test: text search finds neither.

**Tools**
- R5. Two unit controls (length; slope) apply to every figure, including drawings and popups.
- R6. Filter: three lens buttons in one row; pills only after a lens is chosen and only for that lens; counts on options; applied filters as a removable line; evidence regroups by the chosen lens (population group, ICF chapter, or need).
- R7. Controls block no taller than about 100 px on desktop and landscape phone, and about 190 px on a phone, when collapsed.

**Evidence**
- R8. Evidence is an APA reference list, alphabetical by first author's last name (organisation name for corporate authors); each entry opens a popup with the full citation and the list of pages that cite it, and shows "Cited on" under the entry.
- R9. Why it matters is bullets, one or two short sentences each.

**Visual**
- R10. Type: one sans-serif family (Helvetica/Arial class; no web fonts, no monospace), four sizes with one job each in every section: 56 (36 on phones) page title; 24 section headings, headline figures, the question and dialog titles; 16 all body text, table cells, list items and controls; 13 all secondary text (qualifiers, standard names, captions, labels, table column heads). Weights 400 and 700 only. In tables the value is 16 bold, the row label 16 regular, everything secondary 13 regular. Test: computed styles show one family, at most five sizes and two weights.
- R11. Colour: white ground, black text, two greys, hairline grey rules; no yellow or cream tint anywhere; one accent for state only. Test: at most four text colours; no background tints except a light grey for hit rows.
- R12. Structure: numbered section headings with a heavy top rule and consistent spacing; a sticky nav that marks the current section; consistent hover and focus states.
- R13. Grid: a 12-column grid, flush-left text, asymmetric layout (section titles in a left rail, content in the right nine columns), collapsing to one column below about 760 px.

**Responsive and quality**
- R14. No horizontal page scroll at 375, 768, 812x375, 1024, 1280 and 1920 wide; tables restructure on narrow screens; page length budget about 6,000 px at desktop with details collapsed.
- R15. Accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA minimum; project standard per `governance/armature_v3_review.md`; prior site audit `audits/accessibility-audit-2026-05-10.md`). Itemised in section 6a. Each item is a pass/fail test and must pass before a page is shown to the owner.

### 6a. Accessibility requirements (testable)

**Perceivable**
- A1. Text contrast at least 4.5:1 (large text 3:1); non-text UI (control borders, focus ring, chart lines) at least 3:1 (1.4.3, 1.4.11). Check light and dark schemes separately.
- A2. No information by colour alone (1.4.1): a pressed filter, active section or highlighted row also changes weight, underline or a marker; any status uses words, not only a symbol.
- A3. Reflow (1.4.10): usable at 320 CSS px with no horizontal scroll of the page; 200% and 400% zoom without loss of content (1.4.4); user text-spacing overrides do not clip (1.4.12).
- A4. Semantics (1.3.1, 1.3.2): one `h1`; headings never skip a level; data in real `<table>` with `<caption>` or an accessible name, `<th scope>`; lists are lists; reading order equals visual order. When a table is restyled for narrow screens, header association must survive (do not hide `thead` with `display:none` without supplying equivalent names).
- A5. Figures and drawings: every SVG has an accessible name and a text equivalent (a short description plus the data as a table or list); drawing text uses real text so the unit selector and zoom work.
- A6. Language (3.1.1, 3.1.2): `lang` on the page and on foreign-language strings (for example the Japanese standard title).
- A7. Honour `prefers-color-scheme`, `prefers-reduced-motion` and forced-colors (no motion is required by the design; transitions off when reduced).

**Operable**
- A8. Everything works by keyboard alone (2.1.1), no trap (2.1.2), logical focus order (2.4.3), visible focus on every control at 3:1 or better (2.4.7, 2.4.13 where applicable).
- A9. Focus not obscured (2.4.11): a sticky nav must not cover a focused element (use `scroll-padding-top` or avoid sticky).
- A10. Skip link to the main content is the first focusable element (2.4.1); descriptive page title and link text (2.4.2, 2.4.4); section nav marks the current section with `aria-current`.
- A11. Target size at least 24x24 CSS px (2.5.8); the design aims for 44 px on touch. No drag-only interaction (2.5.7).
- A12. Dialogs: native `<dialog>` with `showModal`, a visible and labelled close control, Escape closes, focus moves in on open and returns to the invoking control on close; background inert. Content that appears on hover or focus is dismissible, hoverable and persistent (1.4.13); the design uses click, not hover.
- A13. No time limits and no auto-updating content; filter changes announce the result count through a polite live region (4.1.3).

**Understandable**
- A14. Every control has a visible label and a programmatic name; unit selectors are labelled `select` elements; toggle buttons use `aria-pressed`; accordions are native `details/summary`.
- A15. Consistent navigation and consistent identification of repeated components (3.2.3, 3.2.4); no change of context on input.
- A16. Plain language (COGA): short sentences, no unexplained jargon or codes (ICF and need codes are always shown with their names), the same term for the same thing throughout; abbreviations expanded on first use; values always carry their unit and who they apply to.

**Robust**
- A17. Valid HTML; name, role and state exposed for every custom control (4.1.2); no `title`-only information; no ARIA where a native element does the job.

**Verification before sign-off**
- V1. Automated scan (axe-core and Lighthouse accessibility) with zero violations at the sizes in R14.
- V2. Keyboard-only walkthrough of every task: change units, apply and clear a filter, open and close a value popup and a citation popup, expand a jurisdiction.
- V3. Screen-reader spot check (NVDA with Firefox or Chrome; VoiceOver where available) of the master table, a popup and a filtered view.
- V4. 320 px and 400% zoom pass; forced-colors and dark-scheme pass; printed output readable.
- V5. Record results in an accessibility audit file next to this one. Findings are never self-certified as compliant; a "pass" means the specific tests above passed on the date and build recorded.

### 6b. Known accessibility defects in earlier iterations (do not repeat)
- Narrow-screen CSS hid table headers with `display:none`, breaking column-header association for screen readers (A4).
- A sticky section nav with no `scroll-padding` could obscure focused elements (A9).
- Verification was shown with filled and open circles and a tooltip (`title`) only (A2, A17).
- The Japanese standard title had no `lang` attribute (A6).
- The gradient drawing had only an `aria-label`, no text equivalent (A5).
- Dotted-underline button text for values and citations gave a weak, non-standard link affordance and relied on hover (A1, A8).
- None of the iterations has been run through an automated or screen-reader test (V1-V3).

## 7. Where each iteration stands against this

| Iteration | Strengths | Fails |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Original v2 page (own CSS, three typefaces, tiles, pills, 26 type combinations) | Content depth; units; filters; citations | R10, R11, R12; far too long; horizontal scroll at 768 |
| 2. v3 on the site stylesheet (cream, slab and mono) | Section identity; consistent with the site | Owner dislikes the typefaces and the yellow; sizes poor (R10, R11) |
| 3. Neutral version (white, one sans, numbered heavy-rule sections, sticky nav, hero) | Aesthetics the owner preferred; R10-R12 mostly met | Information order and tables less clear than iteration 4 |
| 4. Article version (Wikipedia-like organisation) | Information order, plain tables, content visible: "better data flow" | Skin: blue links, grey panels and boxes, contents box; owner rejected the look |
| 5. Swiss-grid version (built, not yet reviewed with the owner) | Fits R13 | Untested against R1-R15; not yet judged by the owner |

## 8. Decisions needed from the owner before redesign

- Q1. Typeface: is one neo-grotesque (Helvetica/Arial) the intended Swiss reference, or do you prefer another single sans (for example a system UI sans)? A serif body is off the table unless you say otherwise.
- Q2. Accent: Swiss red for state only, a dark blue, or none (black and grey only)?
- Q3. Dimensions.com: the page I saw is a prose-led collection page. Is there a specific dimension page whose value display you want to match?
- Q4. Lead graphic: do you want a drawing under the hero on every spec page (the draft drew the run needed for the same rise at each gradient from the page's own data)? It carries the data visually but needs a data-driven drawing per item.
- Q5. Sticky section nav: keep it (it gives "dynamic identification") or drop it on short pages?
- Q6. Default state of jurisdiction details and evidence notes: collapsed (shortest page) or expanded?
- Q7. Dark mode: required, or ignore for now?

## 9. Process notes (what I got wrong)

- I restyled five times without a fixed requirements baseline, so each pass answered the last remark and undid an earlier one.
- I applied the site stylesheet before checking whether the owner liked it, and treated "Wikipedia is good" as a skin rather than an organisation.
- I gave weight to references I could not read (Medium, JSTOR, Wiley) as if I had; nothing here relies on them except the saved JSTOR file's design-system facts.

## 10. Doctrine alignment (added after reading the mission and project doctrines)

Documents read: `governance/mission-and-epistemics.md` (CANONICAL), `governance/audience-priority.md` (CANONICAL),
`references/project-standards.md` Core Doctrine, `governance/tier-system.md`.

**Owner definition of best practice (stated in session, matches the Core Doctrine rule):** the Guidebook takes no
positions. Best practice is the best way to do something according to how it benefits the intended group, determined by
the evidence hierarchy, not by code consensus and not by what is most common. For a given item and group the page shows
the most accommodating value found (here the gentlest slope, 1:20, which is gentler than Germany's 1:16.7 maximum) and
whether any study or professional body improves on it. Codes are shown as the regulatory minimum for comparison.

Changes made in the page to match:
- Removed "Guidebook position", "working position", "most common legal maximum" and the steepest-slope figure (owner: do not highlight it). The hero shows the best practice found and the gentlest legal maximum.
- Evidence markers are shown on every value row (project rule: unmarked is an error): the symbol plus the words "evidence-based" or "inferred", with a legend; symbol alone is never relied on (accessibility A2).
- Wording follows the specification-language rule (the project is an advocacy project, not a standard-setting body): no "shall be" or "must"; the person tier reads "An occupational therapist's assessment determines the position within the range"; basis lines say what the standards and studies state.
- Values are marked provisional: the best-practice value rests on standards alone (tier 4 to 6), and no higher-tier study sets a value.
- Populations with no evidence stay off the table (owner instruction) but are named in the Gaps section, so the page is not silent about them.
- The page states that no lived-experience (Co-1) evidence on this item is recorded in the library (checked in the database: 0 Co-1 sources linked to the item's evidence base; the library holds 29 Co-1 sources overall, none on ramps or slopes).
- The controls (lens, filters, units) sit above all information, as the owner required. The question line under the title was removed at the owner's direction ("irrelevant"), so this page no longer carries a question at all.

**Tensions between the owner's instructions and the written doctrine (need an owner decision, not silently resolved):**
1. Evidence-state rule says a cell with sparse evidence displays `[BEST-PRACTICE-PENDING]` with a gap link. The owner said rows that are "Not set" should not show. Current handling: no table row, a plain statement in Gaps. Confirm.
2. Doctrine says tier 4 to 6 are a regulatory baseline "walled off from best-practice anchoring" and that a best-practice claim from standards alone is "in error" when it comes from convergence. The owner's rule (best practice is the most accommodating value stated by a current standard unless evidence improves on it) is implemented as a single-source gentlest value, marked evidence-based but provisional, with the basis stated. Confirm this is the intended reading and whether the marker should be inferred instead.
3. The questions-led commitment ("questions are first-class data") is not met on this page: the owner removed the question line under the title as irrelevant, and there is no "questions to ask" content for E-03 in the data (none invented). Confirm how the questions-led doctrine should appear on specification pages.
4. Audience-priority doctrine names four audiences and use-patterns; the site's exemplar `specs/e-08.html` has a "Reading as" lens that changes which sections open by default. It has not been built into this page. The three owner lenses (population, ICF code, access need) are all present. Confirm whether the audience lens is wanted here.
5. Doctrine requires within-population variability as a first-class dimension; the page shows it only through the person tier and group rows. More is possible once data exists.


Control order (owner, 2026-10-29): the Lens row comes first, then its pills when a lens is chosen, then the Units row; all controls sit above all information.

## 11. Addendum: navigation legibility (owner, 2026-10-30)
Owner: "ensure that minimalism does not come at the expense of readability/legibility especially as it pertains to accessibility practices for website navigation."
- R16. Navigation (breadcrumb, section nav, skip links, disclosure and sort controls) is at least as large and as dark as body text (16 px or larger, near-black on white, or the dark-scheme equivalent); the current location is marked at page load; control state (open, closed, sorted, pressed) is visible without relying on small grey glyphs; targets are at least 44 px high on touch screens. Tenet: minimalism removes decoration, never legibility or state cues.
- Pills are allowed if used judiciously (filter options, applied filters); decorative or status pills remain the trope to avoid.
- Defects against these rules are listed in `audits/spec-page-design-defects-2026-10-30.md` section E.


## 12. Owner answers to the open doctrine questions (2026-10-30)
- Pending cells: unchanged (no "Not set" rows; gaps listed under Gaps).
- Standards as best practice: the owner decided that the gentlest value found in practice is best practice and that no academic study is required; the mission document's tier 4 to 6 wall is therefore superseded in practice and needs a decision record (D-DOCT).
- Provisional means the source reading needs a second review; page wording corrected accordingly.
- "Covered" means read, extracted and verified; the page now says "read, none yet verified" and lists uncovered jurisdictions as "not yet read".
- Two lenses exist: audience and disability. The audience lens is not yet built on the v3 page.
- All spec pages now live in `site/specs/` (the root `specs/` folder was removed; `index.html` links and the e-08 exemplar's relative paths were updated).

content.content:
##### 101
2026-10-30T01:55:32.125Z
**Short answer: no, not yet.** What exists is one pilot page (E-03) plus a written design standard. It shows what a rendered page could look like, but the research-to-page pipeline behind it is not generalised.

I just checked the data layer:
- **Page generator:** only E-03 uses it. The other 88 spec pages in `site/specs/` and `specs/e-08.html` are in older designs.
- **Page content source:** it comes from one hand-written file, `data/spec_pages/E-03.json`, not from the database.
- **Empty database tables:** `source_value_extractions`, `evidence_cell_state` and `convergence_assessment` are all empty, and there is no specification or jurisdictional-value table.

## Concerns

**Generalising**
1. The generator hardcodes ramp-specific logic:
   - the hero and drawing are built from slope and run;
   - the parameter table assumes landings, width, handrails and cross-slope;
   - "best practice = the lowest slope" is a rule specific to this item.
2. Other items need a per-item description of which direction is more accommodating, and none exists. Corridor width, door force, reverberation time, light level and temperature each differ.
3. Units cover only slope and length. Noise, light, force, time, contrast ratio and temperature have none.
4. Several decisions were made for E-03 alone:
   - the 24-jurisdiction scope list is hardcoded in the generator;
   - the 500 mm rise assumption comes from one UK limit.

**Data and traceability**
5. The page's values were typed by me into the JSON from PDFs I read, so nothing in the database records them. That breaks the project's own rule that every handoff must be traceable.
6. There are two copies of each fact, one in the database and one in the JSON, so they can drift apart.
7. 20 older jurisdiction-value files (`data/jurisdictional_values/*.yaml`) have unclear status, and the E-03 one had known defects.
8. The ICF codes, the 14 access needs and every population, ICF and need tag are mine, from migration 026. They are provisional and unreviewed, yet they drive the filters readers see.
9. Evidence entries without a population tag (the healthy-volunteer studies) simply never appear under population filtering.

**Doctrine versus your instructions**
10. The doctrine says a "pending" cell should be displayed with a gap link. You said not to show "Not set" rows. I used a Gaps statement and nothing is confirmed.
11. The doctrine says standards (tiers 4–6) can't anchor best practice. Your rule treats the gentlest standard as best practice until evidence improves on it, and I marked it ● but provisional.
12. The questions-led commitment isn't met on the page.
13. The doctrine names an audience lens (designer, therapist, disabled person, policymaker) and I haven't built it.
14. Within-population variability is barely shown.

**Design and accessibility**
15. I rejected the site's own stylesheet look, so the project now has two design systems.
16. I wrote a requirements document for one page. There is no shared component library or site-wide template yet, and no rule for how the home page and navigation relate.
17. Accessibility is only partly tested: no screen reader, forced colours, 400% zoom or print test, and no third-party scanner.
18. The page is long (8,100 px desktop, about 15,300 px phone) against the 6,000 px budget I set.
19. Landscape phones still show no headline figure on the first screen, because controls come first.
20. Citations aren't fully APA, and the title and hero sit on a different left edge from the section content.

**Process**
21. I restyled the page about six times before fixing requirements. Several defects were my own, for example the table-width bug and the phone layout regression.
22. Both audits are self-authored. The one independent review was visual only.
23. Many "verified" claims come from checks I wrote myself.

## Confusions

1. **Best practice with trade-offs.** A gentler ramp is longer and more tiring in total, and one UK document says so. Who decides, and how, when groups or parameters conflict? The doctrine has a conflict-mapping rule I haven't applied.
2. **Which tier numbering governs?** The mission document, the project standards and `tier-system.md` disagree on what tiers 2 and 3 are.
3. **Where do pages live and what is deployed?** The root `specs/` folder, `site/specs/`, or both? I don't know what the live site serves.
4. **What does "lens" mean?** You use it for population, ICF code and access need. The e-08 exemplar uses it for audience.
5. **Is "buckets 1 and 2" really P1+P2+P3?** I assumed so.
6. **What counts as "covered"?** The page says 15 of 24 are read. The coverage table has 47 codes, and "read from a primary text" for a text-extracted PDF is my judgement.
7. **Should pages come from the database or from curated JSON?** If curated, who reviews it, and when does it become database data?
8. **What is the "specification" the book meant** versus what the item pages now show, and how do they relate to the generated parts files (currently a stub mode with 0 of 82 sources rehabilitated)?
9. **Is a single-source gentlest value acceptable** as "evidence-based" when the library holds no study that supports it?
10. **Is provisional the intended permanent state** for most values, or a stage?

## What the session did clarify
It gives a concrete target: what a rendered page must contain (per-jurisdiction value, clause, edition, tier, read level and link; per-group value with marker; evidence with population, design, sample size and finding; gaps; lived-experience status; a plain-language line). That implies what the research stages must output.

It does not yet turn that into a schema, a database contract, or a generator that works from the database.

I suggest next writing a render contract that maps each page element to the data it needs (existing table, missing table, or manual), and splitting the generator into a general layout engine plus a per-item parameter file. Do you want that, or should I first resolve the confusions above with you?

##### 104
2026-10-30T02:04:15.852Z
Your rest-landing hypothesis is partly supported by the project's documents. The item and the codes treat the rest landing as a design parameter alongside slope, and the page currently buries it. Nothing is committed.

**1. Rest landing versus slope: what the documents say**
- **The book's E-03 spec:** it pairs the slope with a rest provision. The slope is 1:20 on all accessible routes, with a maximum continuous run of 9 m without a rest platform and a level platform of at least 1500×1500 mm at each 9 m.
- **The item's question:** "can someone with MS-related fatigue use this ramp without it exhausting them before they reach the top?"
- **Unsourced claims:** the item's own register (GAP-016) says the 9 m run, the rest platform and the "3× the energy of 1:12" claim have no specific citation.
- **The codes I read:**
  - UK and Ireland say some people need to stop frequently "to regain strength or breath". They add that a high total rise is "unacceptably tiring… even if a number of rest landings are provided", so slope, rise and rests all matter.
  - Maximum run or rise between rests differs widely. Germany allows 6 m, Singapore 6 m at 1:12 up to 15 m at 1:20, Canada and Spain about 9 m, and the UK 500 mm of rise per flight, which is 10 m at 1:20. The US, Japan and New Zealand allow 750–762 mm of rise, which is about 15 m at 1:20.
- **The library studies:** none isolates rest landings. Hashizume 2015, a long ramp at 8% with able-bodied people, found oxygen use and heart rate climbed with distance, ending at "extremely high exercise intensity". That supports distance and uninterrupted length mattering, not slope alone.

Under your rule (the most accommodating value found is best practice), the shortest run between rests found is Germany's 6 m. That reading is from a secondary source, so it is provisional. This means the page currently undersells the parameter you think matters most. The hero, the drawing and the values table show slope only, and landing spacing sits in one table column.

**2. Which tier document is more recent: `governance/tier-system.md`**
- **Dates:** it is dated 2026-05-25 and marked operative, and it records your "t2>t3" directive. The mission document is 2026-04-26 and the old tier lines in project-standards are older.
- **Stale line:** the project-standards line giving tier 2 as NGO/DPO guidelines and tier 3 as systematic reviews is stale.

**3. Folders: consolidated into `site/specs/`**
- **Why that folder:** all three page generators already wrote there, as do the sibling `site/populations/` and `site/rooms/` folders.
- **Moves:** the root `specs/` folder is gone. The new E-03 page and your hand-built e-08 exemplar both moved into `site/specs/`. The e-08 move replaced an older, much smaller generated e-08 page that sat there (git history keeps it).
- **Updated:** the exemplar's relative paths, the six links on `index.html`, and the generator's output folder.
- **Checked:** the pages and stylesheet all resolve at the new paths.

**4–10.** Understood and recorded in memory and the requirements audit.
- **Lenses:** there are two. The disability lens (population, ICF, need) is built. The audience lens, which changes which sections open by default, is not built yet.
- **Page wording:**
  - **Provisional:** "Provisional" now means the source was read once and needs a second review, not that the evidence is weak.
  - **Read vs verified:** the page says "15 of 24 read, none yet verified". The nine others are listed as "not yet read".
  - **Best practice:** best practice rests on the value existing in practice, with no study required.
- **Doctrine decision needed:** your point 9 conflicts with the mission document's rule that tiers 4–6 can't anchor best practice. That needs a doctrine decision record, which I haven't written.
- **Database-direct rendering:** noted as the target. Today the page reads a hand-written file and the database's value-extraction tables are empty.

Should I add rest-landing spacing as a second headline parameter now (hero, drawing and values table), with best practice as the shortest run between rests found? Or commit what's done first?

name: contract-traceability-invariant
description: "Hard requirement for the Guidebook — every boundary/handoff/IO at every stage and layer must have a verifiable, traceable contract."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: d8ad22dd-b407-4f8b-b198-5ff102840966
---

A load-bearing requirement for the Guidebook pipeline: **at every single stage and layer — from the moment a website is visited and something of value is located, through every handoff — there must be a proper handshake/contract.** EVERY handshake / contract / handoff / exchange / input-output MUST be **verifiable** (you can mechanically check the contract held) AND **traceable** (you can follow provenance backward and forward across the boundary).

Boundaries this covers in the current system (non-exhaustive): runtime website request → data lookup → render; migration → DB (`data_migrations` ledger, `content_sha`); DB → Pydantic/JSON schema validation; DB → generated parts/site/vetting-surface; research → evidence collection (citation mining, probes, source/URL verification runs); evidence → judgment (directness, scope, tier, FDR, convergence, evidence_cell_state); judgment → synthesis → collation → rendering; governance DR → attestation JSON; CI gate handoffs.

**Why:** This is the transparency guarantee that makes the output policy-grade and academically defensible (see [[project-end-goal]]). An untraceable or unverifiable handoff is a break in the evidence chain even if both sides are individually correct — it is treated as a defect of the same class as data corruption.

**How to apply:** When auditing or building, enumerate boundaries and for EACH ask: (1) Is there an explicit contract (schema/interface/ledger entry)? (2) Is conformance verifiable by a check, not by trust? (3) Is the exchange traceable end-to-end (provenance preserved, attributable, reproducible)? Any boundary that crosses data without all three is a finding. "Verifiable + traceable at every boundary" is a first-class audit dimension, not a nice-to-have.

**Sharpening — obscured transitions do the most damage.** The highest-risk boundaries are the ones nobody declared as boundaries: implicit couplings, hand-synced duplicate representations (DB ⇄ JSON register kept in sync manually), steps "applied out-of-band" (the ledger-only `data_migrations` rows where SQL was not re-executed), manual handoffs with no record (PI bump that only goes live when the owner pastes into claude.ai), silent field drops in `convert_*` mappings, and identifiers reused with shifted meaning across layers. A declared boundary can be guarded; an obscured one corrupts the chain with no alarm. So the audit must FIND hidden transitions, not just grade the visible ones — actively hunt for undeclared seams and rank them above cosmetically-imperfect declared contracts.

name: project-end-goal
description: "The Guidebook project's true end goal — a multi-modal site that dynamically renders policy-grade weighted evidence from one big data table."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: d8ad22dd-b407-4f8b-b198-5ff102840966
---

The Guidebook (`C:\Github\guidebook`, SQLite-backed at `data/guidebook.db`) exists to produce a **multi-modal website** that dynamically interprets a massive table of data according to user requirements. The data must be sound for **academic viability and policy development**, so the evidence standard is extremely high AND the evidence must carry **dynamic weighting that shifts with user requirements** (not a single fixed score).

It is governed by an overarching mission statement / methodology, realized through an end-to-end pipeline:
**research → evidence collection → judgment → synthesis → collation → rendering → presentation** (stage names approximate; the principle is a transparent chain).

**Why:** This sets the audit bar. "Correct" here means fitness-for-mission, not just clean code: every pipeline stage needs rigorous, portable, transparent data management so the data can be reworked at any stage and the evidence chain stays auditable. The DB-is-source-of-truth + forward-only-migrations + reproducibility design exists to serve this transparency/portability requirement.

**How to apply:** Judge every finding against the pipeline. Ask of any component: which stage does it serve, is its data portable/transparent into the next stage, and does it preserve the dynamic-weighting + provenance needed for policy-grade output? Structural soundness (see the architecture audit) is a *prerequisite*; the higher-order question is whether the pipeline as a whole can render trustworthy, user-conditioned evidence. Relates to [[architecture-audit-2026-06-22]].
